subject: Chemistry
note: Mole-concept drill templates for Teaching/Mole-Concept lessons 0001-0005. Every expr is written for the hand-rolled parser in js/numericals.js: + - * / ^ ( ) , numbers, and the named constants only (N_A = 6.022 x 10^23). There is no eval here, so Math.pow, string literals and JS functions do not work and silently produce NaN. Atomic masses used: H 1, C 12, N 14, O 16, Na 23, S 32, Cl 35.5, Ca 40. Limiting-reagent problems are deliberately absent; they live in chemistry.json and belong to a later lesson.

templates.subject: Chemistry
templates.template: Calculate the amount, in mol, in {m} g of water, H₂O. (H = 1, O = 16 g/mol.)

solutionChain.statement: m = {m} g. Atomic masses: H = 1 g/mol, O = 16 g/mol.
solutionChain.justification: The balance reads grams. The question asks for mol. Those are two different quantities and the molar mass is the only thing that connects them.
Every atom in the formula contributes, and the subscript 2 belongs to hydrogen alone. Written as 18 amu it would be the mass of one molecule; written as 18 g/mol it is the mass of one mole of them.
g ÷ g/mol cancels to mol, which is the check that the division ran the right way round.

misconceptions.statement: Divided the molar mass by the mass.
misconceptions.feedback: The ratio is upside down. Check the unit: g/mol ÷ g leaves mol⁻¹, not mol. Writing the unit on every line catches this before the mark is gone.
misconceptions.whyItFeelsRight: Both numbers look like masses, so the order feels arbitrary when you are moving quickly.

misconceptions.statement: Multiplied the mass straight by the Avogadro constant.
misconceptions.feedback: The Avogadro constant converts mol to particles, never g to particles. The mass has to become an amount in mol first, and that answer would also be a count rather than the mol the question asked for.
misconceptions.whyItFeelsRight: 6.022 × 10²³ is the only large number in sight, so it looks like the one multiplication the question wants.

templates.subject: Chemistry
templates.template: Calculate the amount, in mol, in {m} g of carbon dioxide, CO₂. (C = 12, O = 16 g/mol.)

solutionChain.statement: m = {m} g. Atomic masses: C = 12 g/mol, O = 16 g/mol.
solutionChain.justification: Build the molar mass from the board before anything else happens — it is a mark of its own and it is the number every later line depends on.
The subscript 2 sits on the oxygen, so oxygen contributes 32 g/mol of the total and carbon 12 g/mol.
Mass divided by molar mass is the only arrow from the gram world to the mole world.

misconceptions.statement: Divided the molar mass by the mass.
misconceptions.feedback: Upside down. g/mol ÷ g gives mol⁻¹. The unit on the line is what tells you which way the division goes.
misconceptions.whyItFeelsRight: 44 is the number that was worked out, so it feels like the one that should lead.

misconceptions.statement: Used carbon's 12 g/mol as the molar mass of carbon dioxide.
misconceptions.feedback: That is the molar mass of the carbon atoms alone. The sample is CO₂, so both oxygens are on the balance too and M = 44 g/mol.
misconceptions.whyItFeelsRight: Carbon is the first element named in the formula, and 12 is the number you have used most often.

templates.subject: Chemistry
templates.template: Find the mass, in g, of {n} mol of sodium chloride, NaCl. (Na = 23, Cl = 35.5 g/mol.)

solutionChain.statement: n = {n} mol. Atomic masses: Na = 23 g/mol, Cl = 35.5 g/mol.
solutionChain.justification: This question runs the other way from the usual one: the amount is given and the balance reading is wanted.
Chlorine's 35.5 g/mol is a decimal because chlorine is a mixture of two isotopes. It stays a decimal — rounding it to 35 costs accuracy marks later.
mol × g/mol leaves g. Going back to the balance reverses the arrow, so the operation multiplies.

misconceptions.statement: Divided by the molar mass instead of multiplying.
misconceptions.feedback: n = m ÷ M was applied without being rearranged. Going from mol to g multiplies: mol × g/mol leaves g, while mol ÷ g/mol leaves mol² /g, which is not a quantity that exists.
misconceptions.whyItFeelsRight: n = m ÷ M is the formula you have practised most, so the division comes out automatically.

misconceptions.statement: Used only sodium's 23 g/mol.
misconceptions.feedback: A formula unit of NaCl carries one sodium and one chlorine, so both are on the balance. M = 23 + 35.5 = 58.5 g/mol.
misconceptions.whyItFeelsRight: Sodium is named first and 23 is a whole number, so it is the easier of the two to reach for.

templates.subject: Chemistry
templates.template: How many molecules are there in {n} mol of a molecular substance? (Nₐ = 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹.)

solutionChain.justification: The substance is never named because it does not matter. One mole of anything holds the same number of particles.
The Avogadro constant is a count per mole, so mol × mol⁻¹ cancels and leaves a bare count.

solutionChain.statement: The answer is a count of molecules and carries no unit.
solutionChain.justification: Writing g or mol after a particle count is marked wrong even when the digits are right.

misconceptions.statement: Divided by the Avogadro constant.
misconceptions.feedback: Division is the return journey, from particles back to mol. Going from mol out to particles multiplies, and the answer must be larger than 6.022 × 10²³ whenever the amount is more than 1 mol.
misconceptions.whyItFeelsRight: 6.022 × 10²³ is enormous, so dividing feels like the safe move to keep the answer a sensible size.

misconceptions.statement: Gave 6.022 × 10²³, the count for exactly 1 mol.
misconceptions.feedback: That is the answer only when n = 1 mol. The amount given here scales it: N = n × Nₐ.
misconceptions.whyItFeelsRight: The Avogadro constant is the number the question is testing, so writing it down feels like answering.

templates.subject: Chemistry
templates.template: How many molecules of water are there in {m} g of H₂O? (H = 1, O = 16 g/mol, Nₐ = 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹.)

solutionChain.justification: Grams at one end, a particle count at the other. There is no single formula between them — the road passes through the mole box, and that is worth two separate lines.
The molar mass is built from the atomic-mass board before any arrow is drawn.
First arrow: grams to mol. Skipping it is misconception CH-S06, the missing bridge between the lab bench and the particles.
Second arrow: mol to particles. Two arrows means two lines, and combining them into one loses the method mark even when the final digits are right.

misconceptions.statement: Multiplied the grams straight by the Avogadro constant.
misconceptions.feedback: This is the missing bridge. Nₐ counts particles per MOLE, so it can only be applied after the grams have become mol. Grams × mol⁻¹ is not a count of anything.
misconceptions.whyItFeelsRight: The question says grams and asks for molecules, and Nₐ is the only conversion number given, so it looks like a one-step problem.

misconceptions.statement: Inverted the first step, then multiplied correctly.
misconceptions.feedback: The second arrow is right and the first one is upside down. 18 g/mol ÷ {m} g gives mol⁻¹, so the count comes out on the wrong side. One wrong line costs the whole answer mark here.
misconceptions.whyItFeelsRight: With two numbers and one division, the order is a coin toss unless the units are written down.

templates.subject: Chemistry
templates.template: A sample of carbon dioxide contains {Nmult} × 10²³ molecules. Find its mass in g. (C = 12, O = 16 g/mol, Nₐ = 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹.)

solutionChain.justification: Both numbers carry × 10²³, so that part cancels and the arithmetic is smaller than it looks.
Coming from the particle end is a division. Multiplying by 6.022 × 10⁻²³ instead is the sign-flip error: it is a different operation and it gives a number that fits no unit.
Its own line, its own mark.
mol × g/mol leaves g, which is what the question asked for.

misconceptions.statement: Multiplied by 6.022 × 10⁻²³ instead of dividing by 6.022 × 10²³.
misconceptions.feedback: This is the sign error on the power of ten. Dividing by 10²³ and multiplying by 10⁻²³ look alike on a calculator and are the same move, but multiplying by 6.022 rather than dividing is not. The count is larger than Nₐ here, so the amount must come out larger than 1 mol.
misconceptions.whyItFeelsRight: Both forms of the constant appear in textbooks and the negative power reads as though it has already done the dividing for you.

misconceptions.statement: Stopped at the amount in mol.
misconceptions.feedback: That is a correct middle line and the question asked for grams. One more step, m = n × 44 g/mol, and the marks are complete.
misconceptions.whyItFeelsRight: The hard part of the calculation is finished at that point, so it feels like the answer.

templates.subject: Chemistry
templates.template: How many oxygen atoms are there in {n} mol of sulphuric acid, H₂SO₄? (Nₐ = 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹.)

solutionChain.justification: Read what is being counted before counting it. The question asks for atoms of one element, not for molecules.

solutionChain.statement: Each H₂SO₄ molecule holds 4 oxygen atoms, so n(O) = {n} mol × 4
solutionChain.justification: The subscript multiplies the amount while the sample is still in the mole world. Doing it here, rather than at the end, keeps the line readable.
The Avogadro constant is applied last, to the amount of oxygen ATOMS rather than to the amount of molecules.

misconceptions.statement: Counted molecules rather than oxygen atoms.
misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of H₂SO₄ molecules. Each one carries 4 oxygen atoms, so the oxygen count is four times larger. The subscript in the formula is the whole question here.
misconceptions.whyItFeelsRight: n × Nₐ is the move this topic drills most, and it runs before the wording has been re-read.

misconceptions.statement: Stopped at the amount of oxygen in mol.
misconceptions.feedback: A correct middle line: {n} mol × 4 is the amount of oxygen atoms in mol. The question asked for a number of atoms, so it still needs × 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹.
misconceptions.whyItFeelsRight: The 4 is the clever part of the question, so applying it feels like the finish.

templates.subject: Chemistry
templates.template: A {m} g sample of calcium carbonate, CaCO₃, is analysed. Find the mass of calcium it contains. (Ca = 40, C = 12, O = 16 g/mol.)

solutionChain.statement: m(CaCO₃) = {m} g. Atomic masses: Ca = 40, C = 12, O = 16 g/mol.
solutionChain.justification: A percentage by mass compares one element's contribution with the whole molar mass, so the molar mass has to be built first.
The subscript 3 belongs to oxygen alone, giving 48 g/mol of the total. Calcium contributes 40 g/mol and carbon 12 g/mol.

solutionChain.statement: Calcium's share = 40 g/mol ÷ 100 g/mol = 40.0% by mass
solutionChain.justification: A percentage by mass is one element's share of the molar mass. It is not a count of atoms: CaCO₃ is 40.0% calcium by mass while calcium is only 1 atom in 5.
The share is a fraction of the sample mass, so the answer stays in grams and must be smaller than the sample.

misconceptions.statement: Inverted the share.
misconceptions.feedback: That answer is larger than the sample itself, so a part of the sample would outweigh the whole of it. A percentage-by-mass answer must always come out smaller than the mass you started with.
misconceptions.whyItFeelsRight: 100 and 40 are both on the page and the fraction is written down before it is read.

misconceptions.statement: Dropped the subscript 3 on oxygen: M taken as 40 + 12 + 16 = 68 g/mol.
misconceptions.feedback: CaCO₃ carries three oxygens, worth 48 g/mol, so M = 100 g/mol. Reading the subscripts is the first mark in every molar-mass question.
misconceptions.whyItFeelsRight: One symbol, one number is the habit built by NaCl and H₂O, and a small subscript 3 goes unread at speed.

misconceptions.statement: Used the atom count instead of the mass share: 1 calcium out of 5 atoms.
misconceptions.feedback: Atoms of different elements have very different masses, so a share of the atoms is not a share of the grams. Calcium is 1 atom in 5 and 40.0% by mass.
misconceptions.whyItFeelsRight: Counting the atoms in the formula is quicker than building the molar mass, and both feel like ways of saying 'how much calcium'.

templates.subject: Chemistry
templates.template: A hydrocarbon sample contains {12*k} g of carbon and {k*r} g of hydrogen. (C = 12, H = 1 g/mol.) Find how many hydrogen atoms the empirical formula carries for every one carbon atom.

solutionChain.statement: m(C) = {12*k} g, m(H) = {k*r} g. Atomic masses: C = 12 g/mol, H = 1 g/mol.
solutionChain.justification: The data is in grams and the answer wanted is a ratio of atoms. Those are different worlds and the atomic masses are the only bridge.
Carbon's mass is divided by carbon's own atomic mass — never by the molar mass of the whole compound, which would scale every element equally and leave the ratio unchanged.
Hydrogen's 1 g/mol makes this line look like no work at all, and the mark for it is there anyway.

solutionChain.statement: Divide both amounts by the smaller one, {k} mol
solutionChain.justification: Dividing by the smallest forces that element to 1 and leaves the other as its subscript. A result such as 2.50 is scaled by 2 to give 5, never rounded to 3 — rounding invents a different compound.

misconceptions.statement: Divided the masses directly, without converting to mol.
misconceptions.feedback: A ratio of grams is not a ratio of atoms, because a carbon atom is twelve times heavier than a hydrogen atom. Each mass has to be divided by its own atomic mass first.
misconceptions.whyItFeelsRight: The question gives two masses and asks for a ratio, so dividing one by the other looks like the whole job.

misconceptions.statement: Gave the amount of hydrogen in mol instead of the ratio.
misconceptions.feedback: That is n(H), a correct middle line. The subscript is a comparison between the two amounts, so it needs the division by the smaller one.
misconceptions.whyItFeelsRight: The amount in mol is the number most recently written down, and it is the one the method spends the most time on.

templates.subject: Chemistry
templates.template: A compound has the empirical formula CH₂ and a measured molar mass of {M} g/mol. Find n, the number of empirical units in one molecule. (C = 12, H = 1 g/mol.)

solutionChain.statement: Empirical formula CH₂, measured molar mass M = {M} g/mol.
solutionChain.justification: The empirical formula fixes the ratio of atoms. Only a measured molar mass can say how many of those units make one real molecule, which is why this data always has to be given.
E is the mass of one empirical unit in g/mol. It is not the mass of the molecule, and keeping the two apart is what this question tests.
Both quantities carry g/mol, so the units cancel and n comes out as a bare whole number. A fraction here means the molar mass or the empirical formula was misread.

solutionChain.statement: Multiply every subscript in CH₂ by n to write the molecular formula.
solutionChain.justification: Hydrogen takes the × n as well as carbon. Multiplying only the first element is the classic lost mark in this question.

misconceptions.statement: Divided the empirical unit mass by the molar mass.
misconceptions.feedback: Upside down. The molecule is heavier than one empirical unit, so n must come out as a whole number of 1 or more. A value below 1 means the division ran the wrong way.
misconceptions.whyItFeelsRight: Both numbers carry g/mol, so nothing in the units flags which one belongs on top.

misconceptions.statement: Subtracted instead of dividing.
misconceptions.feedback: n counts how many empirical units fit inside the molecule, and 'how many fit' is a division. Subtraction would leave a mass in g/mol, not a count.
misconceptions.whyItFeelsRight: The difference between the two masses looks like the extra material in the molecule.

misconceptions.statement: Divided by carbon's 12 g/mol instead of the empirical unit's 14 g/mol.
misconceptions.feedback: The unit being counted is CH₂, worth 14 g/mol, and the two hydrogens are part of it. Using 12 g/mol counts carbon atoms rather than empirical units.
misconceptions.whyItFeelsRight: 12 is the number carried over from the empirical-formula work, and CH₂ is mostly carbon by mass.

templates.subject: Chemistry
templates.template: Limestone decomposes on heating: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂. Find the mass of carbon dioxide released from {m} g of calcium carbonate. (Ca = 40, C = 12, O = 16 g/mol.)

solutionChain.statement: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂, balanced. m(CaCO₃) = {m} g.
solutionChain.justification: Say the equation in particles before touching the calculator: one formula unit of calcium carbonate gives one molecule of carbon dioxide. The coefficients count particles and moles, never grams.

solutionChain.statement: M(CaCO₃) = 100 g/mol, so n(CaCO₃) = {m} g ÷ 100 g/mol
solutionChain.justification: Leave the mass world before the ratio is applied. Grams are never allowed into a coefficient ratio — that is misconception CH-S02, the most common error in this whole unit.

solutionChain.statement: Ratio CaCO₃ : CO₂ is 1 : 1, so n(CO₂) = n(CaCO₃)
solutionChain.justification: The ratio line is written out even when it is 1 : 1, because that line carries a mark and because the habit is what protects you when the ratio is not 1 : 1.

solutionChain.statement: M(CO₂) = 44 g/mol, so m(CO₂) = n × 44 g/mol
solutionChain.justification: The product's own molar mass, not the reactant's. The answer is smaller than the limestone because the calcium oxide keeps the rest of the mass.

misconceptions.statement: Read the 1 : 1 ratio as equal masses.
misconceptions.feedback: 1 : 1 means equal AMOUNTS in mol, and never equal masses: 1 mol of CaCO₃ weighs 100 g while 1 mol of CO₂ weighs 44 g. This is the ratio-applied-to-grams error, and a 1 : 1 equation is where it hides best.
misconceptions.whyItFeelsRight: With a 1 : 1 ratio it looks as though nothing needs converting, so the two molar masses appear to cancel out.

misconceptions.statement: Stopped at the amount of carbon dioxide in mol.
misconceptions.feedback: A correct middle line. The question asked for a mass, so it needs the final step m = n × 44 g/mol. Two of the three marks are already earned.
misconceptions.whyItFeelsRight: The ratio was the interesting part of the question, so finishing it feels like finishing the problem.

misconceptions.statement: Used the molar mass of calcium oxide, 56 g/mol.
misconceptions.feedback: CaO is the other product. The question asked for carbon dioxide, M = 44 g/mol. Naming the substance beside every M in your working stops this one.
misconceptions.whyItFeelsRight: Both products come from the same equation and CaO is written first.

templates.subject: Chemistry
templates.template: Hydrogen burns in excess oxygen: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. Find the mass of water formed from {m} g of hydrogen. (H = 1, O = 16 g/mol.)

solutionChain.statement: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, balanced. m(H₂) = {m} g, oxygen in excess.
solutionChain.justification: In particles: two hydrogen molecules and one oxygen molecule give two water molecules. Excess oxygen means the hydrogen alone decides how much water forms.

solutionChain.statement: M(H₂) = 2(1) = 2 g/mol, so n(H₂) = {m} g ÷ 2 g/mol
solutionChain.justification: Hydrogen gas travels as H₂, so its molar mass is 2 g/mol and not 1 g/mol. Using 1 g/mol doubles every later line.

solutionChain.statement: Ratio H₂ : H₂O is 2 : 2, so n(H₂O) = n(H₂)
solutionChain.justification: Equal coefficients mean equal amounts in mol — and never equal masses, because the molar masses are 2 g/mol and 18 g/mol.

solutionChain.statement: M(H₂O) = 18 g/mol, so m(H₂O) = n × 18 g/mol
solutionChain.justification: Mass check: the answer is nine times the hydrogen mass, and the oxygen consumed makes up the difference. Nothing is created and nothing is lost.

misconceptions.statement: Read the 2 : 2 ratio as equal masses.
misconceptions.feedback: The 2 : 2 ratio makes the AMOUNTS equal in mol, not the masses. 1 mol of H₂ is 2 g and 1 mol of H₂O is 18 g, so the water always outweighs the hydrogen it came from.
misconceptions.whyItFeelsRight: Once the coefficients match, it looks as though the conversion steps cancel each other out.

misconceptions.statement: Used 1 g/mol for hydrogen instead of 2 g/mol for H₂.
misconceptions.feedback: The equation is written with H₂ because hydrogen exists as a molecule of two atoms. M(H₂) = 2 g/mol, so the amount is half what this answer assumes.
misconceptions.whyItFeelsRight: The atomic-mass board says H = 1, and the subscript 2 in the equation goes unread at speed.

misconceptions.statement: Brought the excess oxygen into the answer.
misconceptions.feedback: Excess means the oxygen is not the limit, so it never enters the calculation. The question asked for water, M = 18 g/mol.
misconceptions.whyItFeelsRight: Oxygen is named in the question, and data that is mentioned feels as though it must be used.

templates.subject: Chemistry
templates.template: In the Haber process, N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃. Find the mass of ammonia produced from {n} mol of nitrogen, with hydrogen in excess. (N = 14, H = 1 g/mol.)

solutionChain.statement: N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃, balanced. n(N₂) = {n} mol, hydrogen in excess.
solutionChain.justification: In particles: one nitrogen molecule and three hydrogen molecules give two ammonia molecules. The amount is already in mol, so the first conversion step is not needed here.

solutionChain.statement: Ratio N₂ : NH₃ is 1 : 2, so n(NH₃) = {n} mol × 2 ÷ 1
solutionChain.justification: Wanted on top, given underneath, so mol cancels into mol. Two ammonia molecules come from every one nitrogen molecule, so the amount goes up.
The subscript 3 belongs to hydrogen alone.
The excess hydrogen never enters the calculation — the nitrogen alone decides the answer.

misconceptions.statement: Assumed a 1 : 1 ratio.
misconceptions.feedback: The equation says 2NH₃, so every one nitrogen molecule makes two ammonia molecules and the amount doubles. Combining 1 : 1 by default is misconception CH-S01, and the coefficients are on the page to prevent it.
misconceptions.whyItFeelsRight: One reactant and one product are named, so it reads like a straight swap unless the coefficients are read out loud.

misconceptions.statement: Used hydrogen's coefficient of 3.
misconceptions.feedback: The 3 belongs to H₂, which is in excess. The ratio needed is the one between what was given (N₂) and what was asked for (NH₃), which is 1 : 2.
misconceptions.whyItFeelsRight: 3 is the largest and most visible coefficient in the equation.

misconceptions.statement: Applied the ratio upside down.
misconceptions.feedback: Dividing by 2 would mean two nitrogen molecules were needed per ammonia. The rule is wanted over given: 2 ÷ 1, so the amount rises.
misconceptions.whyItFeelsRight: The 2 has to go somewhere and there is nothing in the numbers themselves to say which way up.

templates.subject: Chemistry
templates.template: Sodium hydroxide is neutralised by sulphuric acid: 2NaOH + H₂SO₄ → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O. Find the mass of sodium sulphate formed when {m} g of sodium hydroxide reacts completely. (Na = 23, O = 16, H = 1, S = 32 g/mol.)

solutionChain.justification: In particles: two formula units of sodium hydroxide give one formula unit of sodium sulphate. Two go in for every one that comes out, so the amount will halve.

solutionChain.statement: M(NaOH) = 23 + 16 + 1 = 40 g/mol, so n(NaOH) = {m} g ÷ 40 g/mol
solutionChain.justification: The given substance leaves the mass world first, before any ratio is applied.

solutionChain.statement: Ratio NaOH : Na₂SO₄ is 2 : 1, so n(Na₂SO₄) = n(NaOH) × 1 ÷ 2
solutionChain.justification: Wanted over given, so the amount halves. Applying this 2 : 1 to the grams instead of the moles is misconception CH-S02.
The product's own molar mass, built from the board one element at a time: two sodiums at 23, one sulphur at 32, four oxygens at 16.

misconceptions.statement: Ignored the 2 : 1 ratio.
misconceptions.feedback: Two formula units of NaOH are consumed for every one Na₂SO₄ produced, so the amount of product is half the amount of NaOH. Writing the ratio line before the arithmetic is what earns and protects that mark.
misconceptions.whyItFeelsRight: The mass-to-mole and mole-to-mass steps feel like the real work, so the ratio in the middle is the line that gets skipped.

misconceptions.statement: Applied the ratio upside down.
misconceptions.feedback: Multiplying by 2 would produce more sodium sulphate than there was sodium to make it from. Wanted over given is 1 ÷ 2, so this amount halves.
misconceptions.whyItFeelsRight: The 2 sits in front of NaOH in the equation, so it reads as an instruction to multiply.

misconceptions.statement: Built M(Na₂SO₄) with one sodium and three oxygens.
misconceptions.feedback: Na₂SO₄ carries two sodiums, worth 46 g/mol, and four oxygens, worth 64 g/mol, giving 142 g/mol. Every subscript is worth reading twice in a formula this crowded.
misconceptions.whyItFeelsRight: Na₂SO₄ has more subscripts than any other formula in this question, and they are the last thing added before the answer.

templates.subject: Chemistry
templates.template: A sample of an unknown compound has a mass of {m} g and contains {n} mol. Find its molar mass.

solutionChain.justification: Two of the three quantities in n = m ÷ M are given, so the third is found by rearranging rather than by a new formula.

solutionChain.statement: Rearrange n = m ÷ M to give M = m ÷ n
solutionChain.justification: The same three-term formula. Rearranging it without hesitation is a prerequisite for the whole unit and appears inside longer questions constantly.
g ÷ mol gives g/mol, which is the unit a molar mass must carry. In amu the same number would describe one single molecule instead of one mole of them.

misconceptions.statement: Divided the amount by the mass.
misconceptions.feedback: That gives mol/g, which is the reciprocal of a molar mass. The unit on the line is the fastest check: a molar mass must read g/mol.
misconceptions.whyItFeelsRight: n = m ÷ M is memorised with n on the left, so n leads the division out of habit.

misconceptions.statement: Multiplied the mass by the amount.
misconceptions.feedback: m = n × M is the rearrangement that finds a mass, not a molar mass. Solving for M leaves a division: M = m ÷ n, and the units g × mol do not describe anything.
misconceptions.whyItFeelsRight: m = n × M is the other formula from this topic, and picking the wrong one of the two is quick under time pressure.

templates.subject: Chemistry
templates.template: What volume does {n} mol of oxygen gas occupy at STP? (Molar volume at STP = 22.4 L/mol.)

solutionChain.statement: n(O₂) = {n} mol, molar volume at STP = 22.4 L/mol.
solutionChain.justification: Check the conditions before reaching for 22.4 L/mol: the substance must be a gas and the question must say STP. Applied to a solid or a liquid, or at any other temperature and pressure, it is misconception CH-M06.
mol × L/mol leaves L, which is the unit the answer must carry.

misconceptions.statement: Divided by the molar volume.
misconceptions.feedback: Division is the return journey, from a volume in L back to an amount in mol. Going from mol out to L multiplies, and 1 mol of any gas at STP fills 22.4 L, so the answer here must be larger than the amount in mol.
misconceptions.whyItFeelsRight: 22.4 is the larger number, and dividing by the larger number is the habit built by n = m ÷ M.

misconceptions.statement: Gave 22.4 L, the volume of exactly 1 mol.
misconceptions.feedback: That is the answer only when n = 1 mol. The amount given scales it: V = n × 22.4 L/mol.
misconceptions.whyItFeelsRight: 22.4 L/mol is the fact the question is testing, so writing it down feels like answering.

misconceptions.statement: Multiplied by the Avogadro constant instead of the molar volume.
misconceptions.feedback: Nₐ converts mol to a number of particles, and the question asked for a volume in L. The constant that carries L/mol is the molar volume, 22.4 L/mol.
misconceptions.whyItFeelsRight: Both are 'per mole' constants from the same chapter, and Nₐ is the one drilled most often.
